- If sentiment is strongly bullish (≥0.67) in recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast slope or cap upward momentum.
- If sentiment is bearish (≤0.33) or neutral (0.00), model often underestimates downside risk; add downward bias or widen range for early correction.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >5% from prior peak), model frequently overcorrects with a steep upward trend; cap forecast growth to avoid overshoot.
- When true outcome shows strong mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 consecutive days of decline after peak), model often fails to recognize it; adjust forecast to reflect gradual decline.
- If model forecast is rising steadily but true outcome shows early divergence (e.g., first 3–5 days), reduce forecast slope to align with sentiment-driven volatility.
- For 30-day horizon, model often fails to capture early sharp drops; apply a “lag correction” — delay initial downward movement by 1–2 days if sentiment is negative.
- If sentiment history shows alternating bullish/bearish cycles, model tends to “smooth” transitions; introduce a “sentiment switch” rule to adjust forecast direction at sentiment crossover points.
